main_damage_causes: Compression of Voldemort's historical reign of terror removes the societal scale and named casualties that justify the wizarding world's deep trauma, flattening Voldemort's menace from a decades-long civilizational catastrophe to a generic threat

Harry's active, sustained physical agency in the climactic struggle with Quirrell is diminished—the book's prolonged grapple where Harry deliberately weaponizes his touch is replaced by a more passive crumbling, reducing the demonstration of Harry's hard-won courage

Key thematic and characterization lines are omitted: Dumbledore's 'Fear of a name increases fear of the thing itself' removes the saga's central thesis on fear, and Harry's post-confrontation 'VOLDEMORT!' moment removes his post-ordeal assertion of fearlessness

Loss of the Dippet memory scene removes Riddle's psychological complexity, his backstory, and the Harry-Riddle parallel of orphan desperation, reducing the saga's most important villain to a purely menacing figure at his crucial introduction

Harry's impassioned speech about his mother's sacrificial love is cut from the Chamber climax, removing his most important act of thematic agency and the explicit articulation of love-as-power that underpins the entire saga

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 3 – Hagrid reveals Voldemort's history at the Leaky Cauldron
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Hagrid gives a rich, emotionally textured account: Voldemort gathered followers over roughly twenty years, killed anyone who stood up to him (McKinnons, Bones, Prewetts named explicitly), and specifically notes that James and Lily were Head Boy and Girl, close to Dumbledore, and that Voldemort may have tried to persuade them before killing them. Hagrid weeps openly, blows his nose 'like a foghorn,' and shows deep personal grief. The scale and history of Voldemort's reign of terror is conveyed with specificity.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film compresses Hagrid's account into a few sparse lines: 'Voldemort started ter gather some followers, brought 'em over to the dark side. Anyone that stood up to 'im ended up dead. Your parents fought against him, but nobody lived once he decided ter kill 'em.' The named victims, the twenty-year timeline, the detail about James and Lily being Head Boy and Girl, the emotional weight of Hagrid's grief, and the nuance about Voldemort possibly trying to recruit them are all absent. Hagrid's emotional devastation is significantly flattened.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book establishes Voldemort's reign as a prolonged, society-wide catastrophe with named casualties, giving weight to why the wizarding world is so traumatized. The film reduces this to a generic 'bad guy killed people,' stripping the historical and emotional context that makes Voldemort genuinely terrifying and makes Harry's survival meaningful. It also reduces Hagrid's characterization as someone personally shattered by those dark times.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 3 – Hagrid's account of what happened to Voldemort after Godric's Hollow
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Hagrid says 'Disappeared. Vanished. Same night he tried ter kill you. Makes yeh even more famous. That's the biggest myst'ry, see... he was gettin' more an' more powerful -- why'd he go?' This frames Voldemort's disappearance as a profound, unsolved mystery that haunts the wizarding world.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Hagrid says: 'Well, some say 'e died. Codswallop, in my opinion. Nope, I reckon 'e's out there still, too tired ter carry on. But one thing's absolutely certain. Somethin' about you stumped him that night.' The film has Hagrid offer his own confident theory ('too tired to carry on') rather than presenting the disappearance as a deep, unresolved mystery. Hagrid essentially explains away the mystery rather than leaving it open.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Minor but the book's framing of Voldemort's disappearance as a genuine unsolved mystery adds to the mythology and dread surrounding him. Hagrid volunteering a casual explanation ('too tired to carry on') deflates the sense of awe and mystery the book cultivates.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 7 – Voldemort's face on the back of Quirrell's head reveal and confrontation
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Quirrell binds Harry with ropes, interrogates him about the mirror, and Voldemort speaks independently as a disembodied high voice before the turban is removed. Voldemort's face is chalk white with glaring red eyes and snake-like nostrils. Voldemort makes a philosophically seductive argument ('no good and evil, only power'), taunts Harry about his parents' deaths ('They died begging me for mercy'), then corrects himself and weaponizes Harry's grief ('your mother needn't have died... she was trying to protect you... Now give me the Stone, unless you want her to have died in vain'). Harry shouts 'LIAR!' The physical struggle is prolonged: Quirrell grabs his wrist, Harry discovers his touch burns Quirrell, he grabs Quirrell's face deliberately, then grapples with him for an extended fight while Voldemort screams 'KILL HIM!'
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film has Voldemort speak from the back of Quirrell's head and offer to reunite Harry with his dead parents in the mirror if Harry gives him the Stone. The seductive manipulation via the parents' image is a film invention not in the book corpus. Voldemort's taunts about the parents 'begging for mercy' and the corrective 'your mother needn't have died' are absent. The film's Voldemort says 'There is no good and evil, there is only power' (matching the book's Quirrell quote) but attributes the parents' deaths differently. Harry's active, prolonged physical grappling—grabbing Quirrell's face deliberately as a weapon, the extended struggle, Quirrell screaming while Quirrell's body crumbles under Harry's grip—is replaced by a briefer confrontation where Quirrell crumbles and Voldemort's spirit flies through Harry.
damaging_scenes.explanation: In the book, Harry's victory is active and hard-won: he discovers his touch destroys Quirrell, deliberately weaponizes it, and fights through blinding pain while Voldemort screams. This is a crucial moment of Harry demonstrating courage and agency. In the film, Quirrell's destruction is more passive—Harry touches him and Quirrell simply crumbles. Harry's deliberate, sustained fighting against Quirrell while nearly unconscious with pain is lost, reducing the climax's demonstration of Harry's bravery and active heroism.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 7 – Voldemort's manipulation using James and Lily in the mirror
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book contains no scene where Voldemort offers to resurrect Harry's parents as a bargaining chip. Voldemort taunts Harry about his parents but frames it as mockery and manipulation through grief, not a genuine offer to bring them back. The book's Voldemort says 'Together, we can bring them back' is not in the book corpus.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In the film, Voldemort says 'Would you like to see your mother and father again? Together, we can bring them back. All I ask is something in return.' James and Lily appear in the mirror reflection. This is a film-invented manipulation not present in the book corpus.
damaging_scenes.explanation: While dramatically effective, this invention somewhat softens Voldemort's character from pure domination-seeking malevolence into a transactional manipulator offering gifts. The book's Voldemort is more coldly cruel in his taunts. The change is moderate in damage since Harry still refuses, but it alters Voldemort's characterization and Harry's temptation from grief-exploitation to a false promise.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 7 – Dumbledore's hospital wing explanation of Quirrell's inability to touch Harry
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Dumbledore delivers a rich explanation: 'Your mother died to save you. If there is one thing Voldemort cannot understand, it is love. He didn't realize that love as powerful as your mother's for you leaves its own mark... to have been loved so deeply, even though the person who loved us is gone, will give us some protection forever. It is in your very skin. Quirrell, full of hatred, greed, and ambition, sharing his soul with Voldemort, could not touch you for this reason.' He also tells Harry that Voldemort 'is still out there somewhere, perhaps looking for another body to share... not being truly alive, he cannot be killed. He left Quirrell to die; he shows just as little mercy to his followers as his enemies.' And he delivers the key line: 'Call him Voldemort, Harry. Always use the proper name for things. Fear of a name increases fear of the thing itself.'
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Dumbledore says: 'It was because of your mother. She sacrificed herself for you. And that kind of act leaves a mark. No, no, this kind of mark cannot be seen. It lives in your very skin... Love, Harry. Love.' He also says 'I'm afraid there are ways in which he can return.' The crucial 'Call him Voldemort' / 'Fear of a name increases fear of the thing itself' line is absent from this scene. The detail about Voldemort showing 'just as little mercy to his followers as his enemies' and the characterization of his inability to be killed are also absent or truncated.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The 'Fear of a name increases fear of the thing itself' line is one of the book's defining thematic statements, directly tied to Harry's characterization as someone who refuses to be ruled by fear of Voldemort's name. Its absence removes a key thematic beat. Additionally, the description of Voldemort abandoning Quirrell to die—showing his complete indifference to followers—is important characterization that deepens the villain's menace.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 6 – Hermione's reassurance about Dumbledore and Voldemort
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Hermione's reassurance is: 'Harry, everyone says Dumbledore's the only one You-Know-Who was ever afraid of. With Dumbledore around, You-Know-Who won't touch you.' This is a brief, in-passing comfort amid a broader worried conversation.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Hermione says: 'Who's the one wizard Voldemort always feared? Dumbledore. As long as Dumbledore is around, Harry, you're safe. As long as Dumbledore is around, you can't be touched.' The film makes this a more emphatic, repeated reassurance that is immediately undercut when Dumbledore leaves, which in the film is a more dramatically pointed irony. The repetition ('As long as Dumbledore is around' twice) makes Harry's dependence on Dumbledore more explicit in a way that slightly inflates the Dumbledore-as-safety-net framing.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Minor damage. The repetition slightly over-emphasizes Harry's vulnerability and dependence on Dumbledore rather than his own agency, but the scene's function is essentially the same. Low impact.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 7 – Harry tells Ron and Hermione to go to the Owlery rather than pressing forward with him
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Harry tells Hermione: 'You drink that... get back and get Ron. Grab brooms from the flying-key room, they'll get you out of the trapdoor and past Fluffy -- go straight to the owlery and send Hedwig to Dumbledore, we need him. I might be able to hold Snape off for a while, but I'm no match for him, really.' Harry is cognizant of his limitations and explicitly plans for backup while pressing forward alone.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: After Ron is knocked out, Harry tells Hermione: 'Take care of Ron. Then go to the Owlery. Send a message to Dumbledore. Ron's right. I have to go on.' The substance is similar but the book's Harry explicitly acknowledges he's 'no match' for Snape, showing self-awareness, while also organizing the full retreat plan. The film version is compressed but functionally equivalent in agency terms.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Minimal damage. Harry's agency and decision-making are preserved in both versions. The loss of 'I'm no match for him, really' is a small piece of characterization showing Harry's honest self-assessment that slightly humanizes him, but the omission is minor.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 7 – Harry shouts 'VOLDEMORT!' to assert himself / book's confrontation aftermath with Hagrid
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: After the events, Harry visits Hagrid who is weeping with guilt. Harry shouts 'VOLDEMORT!' at Hagrid to shock him out of his crying, saying 'I've met him and I'm calling him by his name.' This is a powerful character moment showing Harry's hardened resolve post-confrontation and his insistence on naming Voldemort even after having faced him.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: This scene with Hagrid after the confrontation does not appear in the film corpus. The film jumps from the hospital wing scene directly to Harry being reunited with Ron and Hermione.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Harry bellowing 'VOLDEMORT!' at Hagrid post-confrontation is a defining character beat: having actually faced Voldemort, Harry doubles down on his refusal to fear the name. It also provides closure for Hagrid's guilt arc and shows Harry's maturation. Its absence removes a moment of Harry actively demonstrating the courage the book has been building in him throughout the year.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 2 (hospital wing / diary discovery) - Ron's memory of Riddle's trophy excluded per non-theatrical note
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book scenes 38-53: Ron independently recognises T.M. Riddle's name from polishing the trophy during detention, contributing meaningfully to the group's investigation. Hermione deduces the 50-year link through a chain of reasoning that includes Ron's contribution.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Per the non-theatrical exclusion instruction, the scene where Ron recalls Riddle's award from his detention is cut from the theatrical release. In the remaining theatrical film corpus, Hermione drives the diary investigation almost entirely alone, with the trophy-room connection absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Ron loses a small but genuine moment of usefulness and independent recall. The collaborative detective dynamic of the trio is slightly flattened, though the core investigation still proceeds.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 2 (Slytherin common room, Polyjuice sequence) - Draco reveals Chamber history
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book scenes 18-19: Fred and George relay secondhand information about Lucius Malfoy's Death Eater past; the Chamber's history is pieced together gradually. Draco is not presented as a direct source of Chamber exposition for Harry.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film has Draco deliver the key expository fact — that the Chamber was opened fifty years ago and a Mudblood died — directly to Harry-as-Goyle in the Slytherin common room. This compresses the investigative arc and makes Draco an inadvertent informant in a way the book does not.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Minor structural compression. Harry and the trio lose some of the organic, earned quality of their research, but the change is modest and serves pacing. Damage is limited.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 2 (hospital wing diary scene) - Hermione's investigation of the diary
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book scenes 40-53: The trio spend extended time investigating Riddle's diary together — visiting the trophy room, consulting records, and debating theories. Harry is the one most drawn to the diary, almost compulsively returning to it, which foreshadows the Horcrux dynamic. The investigation is collaborative and shows Harry's unusual personal investment.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film condenses the investigation to a single hospital-wing scene driven almost entirely by Hermione (invisible ink theory, Aparecium spell). Harry's compulsive, almost inexplicable attraction to the diary — a key piece of characterisation that hints at his Voldemort connection — is largely absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Harry's strange personal pull toward the diary is thematically important: it seeds the idea that Voldemort's soul fragment resonates with Harry in an unsettling way. Losing this makes the later revelation feel less prepared and reduces Harry's interiority.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 2 (Riddle's memory, corridor/entrance hall) - Riddle's meeting with Dumbledore replaces Dippet scene
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book scenes 83-113: Harry witnesses the full Dippet scene first — Riddle manipulating the headmaster, revealing his orphan background, his half-blood status, his desperation not to return to the Muggle orphanage. This scene establishes Riddle's pathos, his calculated performance, and his motivation. Dumbledore then appears separately in the corridor, recognising Riddle with penetrating suspicion.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film's memory sequence (Film Scene 2, scenes 97-100) cuts the Dippet office scene entirely. Harry arrives in the corridor and witnesses only the brief Dumbledore-Riddle exchange, then follows Riddle to catch Hagrid. Riddle's backstory (orphanage, half-blood status, desperation), his manipulative performance for Dippet, and the full context of his motivation are all absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The Dippet scene is the only place in the book where Riddle's humanity and his tragic backstory are shown in action — the boy who doesn't want to go back to the orphanage, who is pathetic as well as dangerous. It also establishes his skill at manipulation before he shows it on Hagrid. Without it, Riddle in the memory is purely menacing with no psychological complexity. The parallel to Harry ('I don't blame him for wanting to stay') is also lost, which is a meaningful thematic thread.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 2 (Riddle's memory, dungeon) - Aragog's release scene
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book scenes 120-132: Riddle corners Hagrid with a structured, almost legalistic argument ('my word against Hagrid's'), tries to cast a spell at Aragog, and is physically overpowered by Hagrid who seizes his wand. The scene shows Riddle's cold calculation and also Hagrid's fierce protectiveness of his pet.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film scene 100: The confrontation is compressed. Riddle says 'Monsters don't make good pets, Hagrid. Now... stand aside...' and blasts the door. Hagrid leaps on him and they tumble. The key book detail — Riddle attempting to kill Aragog with his wand, Hagrid physically disarming him — is present in rough form, but Riddle's cold rhetorical framing ('my word against Hagrid's... poor but brilliant, parentless but so brave') is absent from the memory; it only appears later in the Chamber confrontation.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Minor loss. The memory sequence still conveys the essential betrayal. The rhetorical self-description is moved to the Chamber scene rather than shown in action, which slightly weakens the sense of Riddle performing victimhood, but the damage is small.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 2 (Chamber of Secrets confrontation) - Riddle's monologue omits key Harry defiance beat
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book scenes 248-250: Harry delivers an impassioned, angry speech explaining that his mother's sacrificial love stopped Voldemort — 'My common Muggle-born mother... She stopped you killing me.' He also taunts Riddle about being 'a wreck', 'barely alive', 'in hiding', 'ugly', 'foul'. This is Harry's most emotionally charged act of defiance and his articulation of why love defeated dark power.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film scene 133: Harry does not deliver this speech. The film moves from Riddle's question about how Harry survived directly to the anagram reveal and then the basilisk. Harry's explanation of his mother's sacrificial protection — and his rage about it — is entirely absent from the confrontation.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is one of Harry's most important moments of agency and thematic articulation in the entire book. He is not just surviving; he is explaining the moral logic of the saga — love as a force that defeats dark power — and doing so with anger and pride about his Muggle-born mother. The film reduces Harry to a largely reactive figure in the Chamber confrontation, and the thematic statement about love's power is lost entirely at the dramatic climax.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 2 (Chamber of Secrets confrontation) - Riddle's curiosity about Harry's survival reframed
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book scene 246: Riddle explicitly tells Harry 'The longer you talk, the longer you stay alive' — he is deliberately stalling Harry's death to extract information about how Harry survived. Riddle's obsessive need to understand the mechanism of his own defeat is central to his characterisation.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film scene 133: Riddle's motivation for prolonging the confrontation is reframed as wanting Harry to watch Ginny die and Voldemort return ('I grow stronger... in a few minutes Ginny Weasley will be dead'). The specific obsession with understanding his own failure is present ('how did a baby manage to defeat the greatest wizard?') but the cold calculation of keeping Harry alive purely to interrogate him is replaced with theatrical cruelty.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Subtle but real. Book Riddle is clinically obsessed with the mystery of his own defeat — it is an intellectual and existential wound. Film Riddle is more conventionally villainous and theatrical. The difference matters because Riddle's inability to understand love-based magic is a core theme.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 2 (Chamber) - Dumbledore's 'abilities vs choices' dialogue altered
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book scene 307: Dumbledore says 'It is our choices, Harry, that show what we truly are, far more than our abilities.' This is the book's explicit thematic statement.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film scene 135: Dumbledore says 'It's not our abilities that show what we truly are, Harry. It's our choices.' The meaning is preserved but the phrasing is inverted. More significantly, the film adds specific Voldemort-associated qualities ('Resourcefulness. Determination. A certain disregard for the rules') that the book does not enumerate, making the parallel to Voldemort more explicit and less troubling.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The core message survives. The film's addition of specific traits is a reasonable dramatisation choice. Damage is minimal.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 2 (Dumbledore's office) - Riddle's self-description ('poor but brilliant') moved from memory to Chamber
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book scene 212: In the Chamber, Riddle delivers his self-justifying speech — 'Tom Riddle, poor but brilliant, parentless but so brave, school prefect, model student' — as a retrospective account of how he framed Hagrid. This speech is devastatingly revealing: it shows Riddle consciously performing victimhood and vulnerability as a weapon.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film scene 133: A version of this is present ('It was my word against Hagrid's. Only Dumbledore seemed to think Hagrid was innocent') but the full self-aware, contemptuous recitation of his performed identity ('poor but brilliant, parentless but so brave') is absent. Riddle's explicit self-awareness about having weaponised his own pathos is lost.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Riddle's gleeful self-awareness about his own manipulation — that he performed the role of deserving orphan and knew he was doing it — is one of the most chilling aspects of his characterisation. It distinguishes him from a merely cruel villain into something more psychologically complex and more directly relevant to the saga's themes about performance, identity, and power. Its absence makes the film's Riddle somewhat less interesting.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 2 (Dobby freeing sequence) - Lucius Malfoy threatens Harry
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book scene 315: After Dumbledore warns Lucius, Malfoy's right hand twitches toward his wand — he visibly considers attacking Harry — before he restrains himself and turns to Dobby. The moment shows Malfoy's barely contained fury and his calculation.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film scene 135A: Malfoy charges at Harry physically after Dobby is freed ('You've lost me my servant!'), and Dobby blasts him away. Malfoy then threatens Harry verbally ('You'll meet the same sticky end as your parents'). The film replaces restrained calculation with overt physical aggression.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Book Malfoy's restraint — choosing not to attack Harry in front of witnesses — is more menacing and more consistent with his character as a political operator. Film Malfoy losing control and physically charging Harry is more dramatically satisfying but less true to the character's cold, calculating nature.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 2 – Mr. Weasley's warning at King's Cross
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Harry overhears Mr. and Mrs. Weasley arguing at the Leaky Cauldron. He is never directly told that Black wants to kill him. Harry pieces the truth together himself by eavesdropping, demonstrating his intelligence and initiative. His internal reaction is notably calm and self-possessed: he is not panicked, is more bothered about losing Hogsmeade privileges, and trusts Dumbledore's protection. He retains full informational agency throughout.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Mr. Weasley pulls Harry aside at King's Cross and explicitly tells him face-to-face that Black is after him and wants to kill him. Harry is a passive recipient of a direct warning rather than an active discoverer of the truth. The scene removes Harry's eavesdropping initiative and his characteristically measured, self-aware response to danger.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book establishes Harry's agency and self-possession as defining traits – he is not a boy who needs to be protected from information, and his calm reaction to learning Black is after him signals his maturity and courage. The film converts this into a conventional 'warned protagonist' beat, flattening Harry's characterization and removing the nuanced internal monologue about fear, Hogsmeade, and Dumbledore's power that rounds out his psychology.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 2 – Harry's vow at the rocky outcrop after Hogsmeade
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book establishes Harry's emotional response to learning about Black's betrayal as complex: anger at Black, grief for his parents, and a particular fury rooted in hearing his mother screaming through the dementors. However, Harry never vows to kill Black. His stated plan is to go after Black (which Ron and Hermione argue against), but the framing is about justice and confronting the betrayer, not premeditated murder. Harry's moral compass remains largely intact.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: After overhearing the conversation in the Three Broomsticks, Harry is discovered crying under his Invisibility Cloak. He explicitly states: 'I hope he finds me. But when he does, I'm going to be ready. When he does, I'm going to kill him.' This is a direct, cold declaration of murderous intent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Harry saying he will kill Black is a significant character distortion. The books are careful to preserve Harry's essential moral goodness even in his angriest moments. The murder vow makes Harry sound ruthless rather than grieving and righteously angry, which undermines the emotional arc of the Shrieking Shack scene – where Harry ultimately spares Pettigrew and refuses to let Black and Lupin become killers – since the film Harry had just declared intent to kill. It also weakens the impact of Harry's mercy in the climax because the contrast with his earlier stated intent is never properly resolved.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 2 – Mr. Weasley's hesitation at saying 'Voldemort'
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book consistently presents Mr. Weasley as a Ministry man who uses 'You-Know-Who' out of ingrained habit and fear typical of the wizarding world. However, Harry's own willingness to say 'Voldemort' is treated as a sign of his courage and his unusual status – modeled on Dumbledore. The contrast between Harry's fearlessness and the wizarding world's terror is a recurring, meaningful beat.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: When Harry says 'Voldemort' twice, Mr. Weasley reacts with visible nervousness and says 'Harry, I hate it when you say –', to which Harry apologizes and adds 'Ron hates it too,' treating it as a social habit rather than an act of courage. The film plays the moment for light humor.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Minor but present: the book treats Harry's use of Voldemort's name as a meaningful marker of courage and his special relationship with Dumbledore's values. The film deflates this into a comedic quirk, losing the thematic resonance, though the damage is limited given it is a brief exchange.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 3 – Lupin's bridge speech about Lily and James
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book's parallel conversation (after the boggart lesson) is focused on Harry's dementor experience, his fear, and specifically the trauma of hearing his mother's voice. Lupin is a careful, controlled mentor who nearly touches Harry's shoulder but stops himself. Harry's emotional vulnerability (tears he hides) and his relationship with his parents' memory are the heart of the scene. Lupin does not deliver an extended personal tribute to Lily.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Lupin delivers a lengthy, lyrical speech about Lily – her kindness, her ability to see beauty in others, her gift for seeing it 'most especially when that person couldn't see it in themselves.' He then pivots to James's 'talent for trouble.' The scene becomes a warm, almost poetic reminiscence with Lupin as the emotional center rather than Harry.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's version of this conversation preserves Harry's interiority – his shame at fainting, his grief, and his specific revelation about hearing his mother's voice. The film transfers emotional weight to Lupin's speech about Lily, which is graceful but reframes the scene around Lupin's feelings rather than Harry's trauma and growth. Harry's hidden tears and the quiet mentor-student dynamic of the book are replaced by a more conventionally moving 'wise teacher' monologue. This softens the rawness of Harry's dementor wound.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 4 – Three Broomsticks: Secret-Keeper revelation without Fidelius Charm explanation
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book's pub scene includes a detailed explanation of the Fidelius Charm from Flitwick, making clear the precise mechanics of how Black's betrayal worked. This is important for audience understanding of why the betrayal was so devastating – James chose Black over Dumbledore's instincts – and for the later revelation that Pettigrew was the real Secret-Keeper.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: McGonagall's account in the film skips the Fidelius Charm mechanics entirely. The film simply establishes that Black 'told You-Know-Who' where the Potters were hiding, without explaining the charm that made Black's betrayal (or Pettigrew's substitution) structurally significant.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Without the Fidelius Charm explanation, the later twist that Pettigrew was the real Secret-Keeper loses some of its logical weight. The audience understands the emotional betrayal but not the precise magical mechanism that makes the swap meaningful. This is moderate structural damage to the mystery's architecture.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 5 – Shrieking Shack: Harry disarms Snape and takes charge
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Harry, Ron, and Hermione collectively disarm Snape by shouting 'Expelliarmus' simultaneously. It is a joint act of the trio. Harry's decision-making in the Shack is present but it is emphatically a group action at key moments.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Harry alone disarms Snape with 'Expelliarmus' after retrieving his wand from the table. It is a solo act. Ron and Hermione stare in shock rather than participating.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The trio's collective agency is a consistent book value – their friendship and combined action repeatedly saves the day. Converting the group disarming into a solo Harry moment marginally diminishes Ron and Hermione's active roles and the relational dynamic of the trio as collaborators rather than Harry as solitary hero.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 5 – Shrieking Shack: Pettigrew's 'Lily and James' speech and Black's confrontation of betrayal compressed
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book devotes substantial space to Black's detailed, venomous exposure of Pettigrew's cowardice and opportunism: 'I'll never understand why I didn't see you were the spy from the start. You always liked big friends who'd look after you.' Black also establishes that he suggested Pettigrew as Secret-Keeper as a bluff, believing Voldemort would come after him instead. Pettigrew's systematic moral cowardice is dissected at length by Black and Lupin, giving the accusation full dramatic weight.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The confrontation is significantly compressed. Black states 'Died! Died rather than betray my friends!' as his primary condemnation. The detailed unpacking of Pettigrew's psychology, the bluff strategy, and Black's self-recrimination for suggesting Pettigrew as Secret-Keeper are absent. Pettigrew appeals to 'what would you have done, Sirius?' and the scene moves quickly.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The extended confrontation in the book serves multiple functions: it establishes Black's moral clarity and grief, explains the precise logic of the betrayal, and reveals the tragic irony that Black's own plan backfired. Compression loses the psychological depth of both Black's character and Pettigrew's villainy, reducing a rich moral reckoning to a faster plot beat.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 6 – Patronus scene: Harry believes his father is coming
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Harry sees a distant figure conjure the powerful Patronus and initially believes it is his father. When he travels back in time and conjures it himself, he has a moment of self-recognition: he knew no one was coming because he was always going to do it himself. His realization is an act of self-discovery and internal courage – he steps into his father's role consciously.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Harry explicitly and repeatedly says 'My Dad will come... he'll conjure the Patronus... any minute... He will come!' with intense conviction. Hermione corrects him ('No one's coming, Harry'). Harry's face then changes and 'a riddle unravels' before he acts. The film preserves the basic beat but frames Harry's initial belief as more desperate and prolonged, with Hermione having to force the realization.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book gives Harry an internal moment of recognition and self-discovery – he realizes he was the caster and steps forward from his own insight. The film makes Hermione's correction ('No one's coming!') the external trigger that breaks Harry's delusion, reducing Harry's self-actualization to a response to Hermione's intervention. The damage is moderate: the core courage is still Harry's, but the interior agency that makes the moment thematically resonant – Harry becoming his father, on his own terms – is partially externalized.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 – Riddle House opening: Wormtail's motivation for suggesting a substitute
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 37-51: Wormtail delivers a sustained, multi-beat argument that the plan could be done without Harry Potter, offering to fetch a substitute wizard. Voldemort probes and exposes Wormtail's cowardice and desire to desert, accusing him of flinching and shuddering when touching his master. Wormtail's sulky resentment ('I found you'), his terror, and his complex mix of self-interest and servility are all on display. The exchange reveals Voldemort's psychological dominance and Wormtail's inner conflict.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 1: Wormtail's suggestion is reduced to a single throwaway line ('if we were to do it without the boy…'), immediately shut down by Voldemort ('No! The boy is everything!'). None of Wormtail's extended argument, Voldemort's psychological dissection of Wormtail's cowardice, or Wormtail's sulky defensiveness ('I found you') is present. The entire exchange is collapsed into two lines.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's extended exchange establishes Voldemort's cold psychological cruelty, his ability to see through and weaponise others' weaknesses, and Wormtail's complex servility. Collapsing it to two lines removes a key early characterisation beat for both characters and strips the opening scene of its psychological tension.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 – Riddle House opening: Voldemort's physical state and dependency
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 22-68: Voldemort is described as inhabiting a rudimentary body, too weak to act alone, needing to be fed ('I will need feeding in the night'), needing Nagini milked, and acknowledging 'a few days alone would be enough to rob me of the little health I have regained.' His current helplessness is a crucial dramatic contrast with his eventual resurrection.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 1: Voldemort's physical dependency and helplessness in his temporary body are entirely absent. He is heard only as a disembodied cold voice before his resurrection at the graveyard. The interim body/state is never shown or described.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The contrast between Voldemort's current frailty and his restored power is dramatically important. Losing it diminishes the sense of his resurrection as a transformative, fearful event and removes context for why the ritual was so urgently needed.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 – Riddle House opening: Bertha Jorkins's fate and plot context
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 52-65: Wormtail explicitly raises Bertha Jorkins's disappearance as a risk ('Bertha Jorkins' disappearance will not go unnoticed for long'). Voldemort explains he killed her after breaking her memory charm and extracting information, noting it would be 'an insult to her memory not to use the information.' This establishes the chain of intelligence that enabled the whole plan and Voldemort's casual murderousness.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 1: Bertha Jorkins is never mentioned in the Riddle House scene. The audience gets no context for how Voldemort learned about the Triwizard Tournament or the identity of his servant at Hogwarts from this opening scene.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's opening efficiently seeds Bertha Jorkins as the information source that made the plan possible, and demonstrates Voldemort's cold, utilitarian attitude to murder. Removing this weakens the logical coherence of Voldemort's scheme as revealed in the film and loses an early demonstration of his calculating murderousness.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 – Riddle House opening: Voldemort references a 'faithful servant at Hogwarts'
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 68: Voldemort says 'my faithful servant at Hogwarts … Harry Potter is as good as mine.' This is a deliberate, ominous plant for the Barty Crouch Jr. revelation.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 1: A mysterious third figure ('Mysterious Man') says 'I will not disappoint you, my Lord,' with Voldemort instructing him to 'gather our old comrades. Send them a sign.' While a third figure is present, the film does not include the specific 'faithful servant at Hogwarts' line that plants the mystery.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Minor structural seed is softened; the film does gesture toward the third figure, but the specific Hogwarts-servant plant is absent, slightly reducing the foreshadowing payoff when Barty Crouch Jr. is revealed.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 9 – Graveyard: Voldemort's speech to the Death Eaters (missing Lestranges, Azkaban promise, giant/dementor recruitment)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 313-354: Voldemort's graveyard address is extensive. He honours the Lestranges ('entombed in Azkaban … faithful'), announces that dementors will join him, that he will recall the banished giants, that he will have 'an army of creatures whom all fear.' He individually addresses Macnair, Crabbe, Goyle, Nott, and reflects on the six missing Death Eaters, including 'one who remains my most faithful servant … already reentered my service.' He explains in detail how he survived and returned, including possessing animals and the Quirrell episode.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 9: Voldemort's graveyard address is heavily compressed. He unmasks Death Eaters (Crabbe, Macnair, Goyle, Lucius), expresses disappointment that none sought him, grants Wormtail a hand, then moves to Harry. The promises about dementors, giants, the Lestranges, the Quirrell backstory, and the detailed accounting of six missing Death Eaters are absent. The revelation about 'the most faithful servant at Hogwarts' already being in place is absent from the speech.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Voldemort's graveyard monologue is the audience's fullest window into his strategic thinking, his forces, and his worldview. Cutting the Lestranges, dementor/giant recruitment plans, and the Quirrell backstory reduces the sense of his broader menace and the scale of the threat being rebuilt. The saga-level stakes of his return are diminished.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 9 – Graveyard: Voldemort's full backstory monologue to Death Eaters (Quirrell, Albania, Wormtail's journey)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 363-389: Voldemort delivers a detailed first-person account of his survival: existing as less than a ghost, inhabiting animals (shortening their lives), possessing Quirrell, being thwarted by Harry, returning to hiding, Wormtail's return, Bertha Jorkins's capture and interrogation, and the full mechanics of how the plan to use the Triwizard Tournament was conceived. This is Voldemort's only extended self-narration across the saga at this point.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 9: None of this backstory narration occurs. Voldemort's explanation to Harry is limited to a brief, direct address about Lily's sacrifice and old magic ('It was love … I could not touch him'). The mechanics of his survival, his time in Albania, Quirrell, and the intelligence chain are entirely absent from the film's graveyard sequence.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This monologue is structurally essential: it is the first and most complete account Voldemort gives of himself, his philosophy of immortality, and his path back to power. Its absence means the audience never hears Voldemort explain himself on his own terms, which is a significant loss to his characterisation as an intelligent, self-aware, and strategically patient villain. It also removes the confirmation of Quirrell's fate and the Bertha Jorkins chain, leaving the film's plot partially unexplained.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 9 – Graveyard: Voldemort's taunting of Harry during the duel ('obedience is a virtue')
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 399-418: Voldemort taunts Harry at length during the duel, using the Cruciatus Curse and then demanding verbal submission ('You don't want me to do that again, do you?'). He applies the Imperius Curse to force Harry to answer, lectures on obedience, and uses Harry's refusal to submit as an occasion to demonstrate his cruelty and Harry's courage. Harry's decision to stand and fight rather than die crouching is an explicit act of agency modelled on his father's death.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 9: Voldemort does cast Crucio twice and taunts Harry ('Your parents would be proud. Especially your filthy Muggle mother'), but the extended Imperius Curse application, the 'obedience is a virtue' lecture, and the sustained psychological pressure are absent. The film also adds the taunt about Harry's 'filthy Muggle mother,' which has no book basis in this scene.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's duel shows Voldemort as a sadist who wants submission and spectacle, not just death. The film's Voldemort is cruder ('filthy Muggle mother') — an invented insult that replaces the book's more calculated psychological cruelty. The loss of the Imperius moment also removes a callback to Moody's earlier lesson. The added insult is out of character with book Voldemort's cold, aristocratic contempt.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 9 – Graveyard: Voldemort adds insult 'filthy Muggle mother'
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 399-418: In the book duel, Voldemort does not use the phrase 'filthy Muggle mother.' His taunts are cold and psychological ('straight-backed and proud, the way your father died'). His references to Lily are analytical (she provided a protection he had not foreseen) rather than derogatory.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 9: Voldemort says 'Your parents would be proud. Especially your filthy Muggle mother.' This is an invention not present in the book corpus.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Book Voldemort's cruelty is cold, measured, and intellectual. The addition of a crude racial slur makes him sound like a common bully rather than the terrifyingly composed Dark Lord of the books. It slightly misrepresents his register and the nature of his contempt.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 9 – Graveyard: Voldemort's interaction with Cedric's corpse
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book corpus: Voldemort ignores Cedric's corpse entirely after the killing, focused wholly on the ritual and Harry. Cedric's death is cold and functional ('Kill the spare').
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 9: Voldemort crouches and touches Cedric's corpse, saying 'Oh, such a handsome boy' before Harry shouts 'Don't touch him!' This is not in the book corpus.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The added moment gives Voldemort a theatrically sinister quality that verges on camp, which is at odds with the book's depiction of him as coldly indifferent to Cedric's body. It slightly distorts his characterisation toward performative villainy rather than chilling detachment.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 3 – Sirius's fireplace conversation: Sirius's assessment of Barty Crouch Sr.
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 182-191: In Sirius's extended cave conversation, he gives a detailed, nuanced account of Barty Crouch Sr. — his rise, his harsh measures against Voldemort's supporters, his authorising of Unforgivable Curses, his fall from grace due to his son's arrest, and the question of whether his principles were ever genuine. This is a significant political and moral portrait.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 3: Sirius's fireplace conversation is severely compressed. He mentions Karkaroff as a former Death Eater and Crouch as having 'sent his own son to Azkaban' with a 'heart of stone,' but the entire nuanced portrait of Crouch's political career, his authoritarian methods, and the moral ambiguity of his anti-Voldemort campaign is absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book uses Sirius's account of Crouch to explore how fear of Voldemort corrupted even those fighting him — a key thematic point. The film's reduction to 'heart of stone, sent his son to Azkaban' loses this moral complexity and makes the Crouch backstory purely a plot point rather than a thematic one.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 7 – Dumbledore's office / Pensieve: Harry's dream report omits Wormtail's blunder and the owl
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 236-245: Harry reports to Dumbledore that in his dream Voldemort tortured Wormtail for a blunder, that an owl brought good news (the blunder repaired, someone dead), that Wormtail would not be fed to the snake but Harry would be. Dumbledore takes this seriously and shares his theory about the scar.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 7: Harry tells Dumbledore he dreamed of 'a house … Voldemort … not quite human … Wormtail … and Mr. Crouch's son.' The specific details of the owl, the blunder, and Voldemort's threat to feed Harry to the snake are not reported. The conversation is brief and focused on establishing Crouch Jr.'s presence.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Minor: the film simplifies the dream report but retains the core function of connecting Harry's scar-visions to Voldemort's plans. The loss of specific details slightly reduces the sense of the scar as a reliable intelligence channel.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 11 – Barty Crouch Jr. revelation: Dumbledore's confrontation and Crouch Jr.'s confession
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book corpus (Crouch Jr.'s confession via Veritaserum, Scenes 480-486): Crouch Jr. gives a detailed account of his escape from Azkaban, his father's Imperius, his infiltration of Hogwarts, and his devotion to Voldemort. Dumbledore then shares this with Fudge and argues urgently for immediate action — reaching out to giants, removing dementors, sending envoys. Fudge's denial and the political confrontation are extensive.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 11: Crouch Jr.'s confession under Veritaserum is implied but not shown in detail. The film cuts directly to Dumbledore's leaving feast speech. The extended Dumbledore–Fudge confrontation (giants, dementors, immediate action) is entirely absent from the film corpus.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The Dumbledore–Fudge confrontation is structurally critical: it establishes the political stakes for the next three books, Fudge's denial, and Dumbledore's immediate strategic response to Voldemort's return. Its absence from the film means the audience does not see Dumbledore take command, argue for action, or have his authority challenged — all of which define his arc going forward. This is a significant saga-level loss.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 12 – Leaving feast: Dumbledore's speech compressed, political context absent
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 547-555: Dumbledore's leaving speech names Voldemort explicitly as Cedric's murderer, acknowledges Ministry opposition, invokes the theme of unity across schools, warns of dark times, and ends with the 'choice between what is right and what is easy' formulation. It is a full political and moral address.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 12: Dumbledore's speech is present and broadly faithful, including naming Voldemort as Cedric's murderer, the Ministry's wish to suppress it, and the bonds of friendship. The 'right and what is easy' line is present in his later private conversation with Harry rather than the feast. The film version is shorter but captures the main beats.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Minor: the film retains the core of Dumbledore's speech. Some compression is present but the essential characterisation and thematic content survive. Low damage.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 — Grimmauld Place briefing: Sirius tells Harry about Voldemort recruiting and a weapon
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book scenes 35-55: Harry asks a sustained, eager series of questions about Voldemort's whereabouts, plans, why he has stopped killing, how the Order is countering him, and what 'something he didn't have last time' means. The conversation is long, detailed, and shows Harry's intellectual hunger to understand the threat. Multiple adults answer in turn (Sirius, Lupin, Bill, Tonks, Mr Weasley). Harry's arrival at the Burrow/Grimmauld Place is framed as his first real information after weeks of frustration.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film condenses the entire briefing into a brief exchange where Sirius says Voldemort is 'recruiting' and 'after something he didn't have last time,' then Molly shuts it down. Harry's questions are minimal. The texture of Harry's intellectual curiosity, the political explanation about the Ministry suppression campaign, Fudge's motives, the Death Eater infiltration concerns, and the Order's counter-strategy are all absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This scene is Harry's re-entry into the wizarding world after isolation and is meant to establish his active, questioning role as someone who has earned the right to information. The film strips this agency, making Harry a passive recipient of a two-sentence briefing rather than a character who fights for understanding. It also removes critical context about Ministry politics that underpins the entire film's conflict.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 — Harry's arrival anger: shouting at Ron and Hermione
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book scene 19: Harry's outburst at Ron and Hermione ('SO YOU HAVEN'T BEEN IN THE MEETINGS…WHO SAVED THE PHILOSOPHER'S STONE?') is a sustained, specific, multi-sentence eruption of accumulated grievance. It is immediately followed by shame and self-awareness, and is framed as the product of weeks of enforced isolation and feeling forgotten by Dumbledore.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film has Harry deliver a compressed complaint ('I'm the one who saw Voldemort return; I'm the one who fought him; I'm the one who saw Cedric Diggory get killed') in a controlled, measured tone rather than a genuine outburst. Fred and George defuse it with humour almost immediately. The rawness and the specific grievances about Dumbledore's exclusion are softened.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Harry's anger in the book is ugly and uncomfortable and that is the point — it establishes the emotional wound of isolation that drives his behaviour throughout OotP. Softening it into a more sympathetic complaint undercuts the psychological portrait the book builds around his 'difficult' year.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 — Harry's internal isolation and summer suffering (opening)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book scenes 1-9: The opening pages establish Harry's sustained psychological state over four weeks — hopelessness, the nightmares about Cedric, the recurring corridor dreams, the scar prickling, the sense of abandonment by Dumbledore, Ron and Hermione, the injustice of being excluded from news. This is an extended, carefully constructed portrait of a teenager on the edge.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film opens with Harry on a swing, briefly tagging Dudley's gang, and moves almost immediately to the Dementor attack. The weeks of psychological deterioration, the specific texture of his abandonment feelings, the nightmares, the Daily Prophet obsession, and his resentment of Dumbledore's silence are entirely absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's entire emotional arc — Harry's anger problem being rooted in weeks of real, justified suffering and exclusion — requires this foundation. Without it, Harry's anger throughout the film reads as a character flaw rather than a comprehensible psychological response to genuine mistreatment. The adaptation loses the justification for his 'difficult' behaviour.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 3 — Umbridge's detention and the blood quill
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book scenes 94-99: After Harry says 'Voldemort killed him' in class, he is sent to Umbridge's office. He refuses to recant and endures the blood quill silently. He chooses not to tell Dumbledore or McGonagall, partly out of stubbornness and partly out of a sense that telling tales would be defeat. McGonagall warns him to keep his head down. Harry consciously accepts the pain rather than capitulate.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film shows the blood quill scene but Harry's internal reasoning for endurance — his refusal to give Umbridge the satisfaction, his deliberate choice — is communicated only through a brief exchange with Ron and Hermione where he says 'I don't want to give Umbridge the satisfaction.' His agency in the decision is present but stripped of psychological depth.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book version shows Harry making a morally complex choice — accepting pain as a form of defiance. The film renders it as stubbornness without fully conveying the principled logic underneath, slightly flattening his characterisation at a key moment.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 4 — Occlumency lessons: Snape's memory of James bullying him
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book scenes 297-304: Harry accidentally sees Snape's memory of being bullied by James and Sirius as a teenager (the 'Worst Memory'). Harry is deeply disturbed — his father is behaving cruelly and he cannot reconcile this with his idealised image. He also sees young Snape's humiliation. He later reflects on this at length. Snape ends the lessons in fury. The scene is pivotal for Harry's understanding of his father's moral complexity.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film shows Harry seeing James cast Expelliarmus at Snape and mock him ('Right, who wants to see me take off Snivelly's trousers?'). Snape then throws Harry out. The scene is present but Harry's emotional aftermath — his crisis over his father's character, his inability to process what he saw — is absent. The film moves directly on without dwelling on the moral weight.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is one of the few moments in the saga where Harry's idealisation of his father is genuinely challenged. The book spends time with Harry's discomfort and unresolved feelings. The film treats it as plot incident rather than a formative crack in Harry's self-understanding, losing the nuance that feeds into his later relationship with Snape and his father's legacy.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 4 — Snape's characterisation during Occlumency: 'Your father was a swine'
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book scene 305: Snape's fury when Harry sees his memory is about violated privacy and humiliation. His contempt for Harry is always about Harry being a symbol of James's triumph. The book is careful to show Snape's cruelty as intelligible even when not excusable.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film has Snape say 'Your father was a swine' directly to Harry's face after Harry defends James. While the book's Snape absolutely holds this view, having him state it so baldly and directly to a student in this moment shifts his characterisation toward cartoonish villainy rather than the book's more controlled, cold cruelty.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Snape's menace in the books comes from what is left unsaid and from restraint deployed as weapon. The blunt declaration diminishes the psychological texture of his antagonism and makes him easier to dismiss as simply a bully rather than the complicated figure the saga requires him to be.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 4 — Luna's explanation of Voldemort's strategy ('if it's just you alone, you're not as much of a threat')
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book does not give this insight to Luna. Harry's dawning awareness of Voldemort's strategy of isolation comes gradually through his own experience and Dumbledore's later explanation. Luna in the books is not characterised as someone who offers political/strategic insight about Voldemort.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film gives Luna the line: 'Well, if I were You-Know-Who, I'd want you to feel cut off from everyone else, because if it's just you alone, you're not as much of a threat.' This is strategic political analysis delivered as wisdom.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Minor but present: the film uses Luna to deliver thematic exposition that the book leaves for Harry to arrive at experientially. It slightly mischaracterises Luna's voice (dreamy and oblique, not strategically analytical) while also short-circuiting Harry's own process of understanding.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 4 — DA formation meeting at the pub
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book scenes 136-142: Harry's meeting at the Hog's Head is tense and adversarial. Zacharias Smith challenges Harry directly and persistently. Harry refuses to perform or justify himself ('I saw him. But Dumbledore told the whole school what happened last year, and if you didn't believe him, you won't believe me, and I'm not wasting an afternoon trying to convince anyone'). Harry is frustrated that Hermione has put him on display. His authority in the room is earned through controlled refusal to pander.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film's pub meeting has a boy challenge Harry but Harry responds with a brief, relatively calm account of his qualifications (Patronus, Basilisk, Dementors, Voldemort in the flesh) before giving a speech about real danger vs classroom danger. He is more openly persuasive and motivational. The adversarial undercurrent and Harry's specific controlled fury at being treated as a curiosity are softened.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book version shows Harry's authority as reluctant and defensive — he will not perform heroism on demand. The film version edges him toward a conventional 'inspiring leader' speech mode, which contradicts the book's careful portrait of a teenager who hates being a symbol.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 4 — Harry's self-doubt speech at DA ('most of that was just luck')
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book scene 128: Harry's breakdown ('You don't know what it's like!') is an angry eruption, not a measured self-deprecating speech. He is furious at being treated like a clever boy for surviving, and his pain about Cedric and nearly dying is raw and uncontrolled. Hermione is the one who calms him by finally saying Voldemort's name for the first time.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film has Harry deliver a quieter, more considered speech: 'the truth is, most of that was just luck... Facing this stuff in real life is not like school.' It is emotionally affecting but controlled and almost pedagogical. The rage, the guilt about Cedric, and the uncontrolled quality are absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's version of this moment is a defining character beat: Harry's anger problem is shown to have a legitimate wound at its core. The film converts it into a modest disclaimer speech, which is more palatable but loses the psychological rawness that justifies the entire arc of Harry's 'difficult' year in the book.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 4 — Harry's conversation with Sirius about becoming like Voldemort (Christmas at Grimmauld Place)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book does not contain a scene where Harry explicitly asks Sirius whether the connection with Voldemort means he is 'becoming bad.' Harry's fears about possession are internal (book scenes 182-191) and he discusses them with Ginny and Hermione, not Sirius in this direct form. Ginny's crucial intervention — telling Harry that being possessed by Voldemort feels like not remembering — is a key book scene.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film has Harry directly tell Sirius: 'I was the snake... this connection between me and Voldemort, what if the reason for it is that I am becoming more like him? What if I'm becoming bad?' Sirius is the confidant for this existential fear. Ginny's role in reassuring Harry about possession is absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Ginny's intervention in the book is a critical moment for her character — she alone can speak from experience of Voldemort's possession — and for Harry's respect for her. Transferring this function to Sirius collapses Ginny's most important character scene in the novel and weakens the basis for Harry and Ginny's eventual relationship. It also makes Harry less independently thoughtful, since the book version has him work through the question over time rather than immediately externalising it.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 6 — Harry's vision of Sirius being tortured triggers the mission
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book scenes 305-325: Harry sees a vision of Sirius being tortured by Voldemort. He immediately wants to act. Hermione raises multiple rational objections (it could be a trick, Voldemort knows Harry's weakness for heroics, how would Voldemort and Sirius even be at the Ministry). Harry and Hermione argue at length. Harry acknowledges some of her points but overrides them because he cannot accept the risk of Sirius dying. The tension is sustained and Harry's decision is shown as emotionally driven and potentially reckless.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film compresses this into a brief exchange. Hermione says 'What if Voldemort meant for you to see this?' Harry replies 'I'm supposed to just let him die? Hermione, he's the only family I've got left.' The decision is made quickly. The sustained rational pushback and the moral complexity of Harry choosing to act on incomplete information are largely absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book version is crucial to the arc: Harry makes a choice that turns out to be catastrophically wrong, and the tragedy of Sirius's death is partly Harry's fault. This is set up by showing his inability to engage with Hermione's logic. The film's shortcut makes the decision feel more reasonable, which softens the devastating lesson Harry must learn about the consequences of acting on unverified emotion.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 8 — Sirius's final words: 'Nice one, James!'
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book does not give Sirius any final words before he falls through the veil. He is hit by a curse mid-battle. The 'Nice one, James' line does not appear in the book corpus provided.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: After Harry casts Expelliarmus and disarms a Death Eater, Sirius says 'Nice one, James!' — confusing Harry with his dead father — before being killed by Bellatrix. This is the film's invention.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The film's addition introduces a poignant but narratively misleading note: it implies Sirius was mentally slipping and confusing Harry with James, which the book never suggests. More damagingly, it reframes the Harry-Sirius relationship in its final moment as one filtered through James rather than direct. The book's Sirius sees Harry clearly; the film's Sirius dies seeing a ghost. This is a significant alteration to the emotional truth of the relationship.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 8 — Harry attempts Cruciatus on Bellatrix
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book scene 365: Harry attempts the Cruciatus Curse on Bellatrix after Sirius dies. He shouts 'Crucio!' in rage. Bellatrix explains that he has to mean it — to really want to cause pain — and that he doesn't hate enough. This is a key moral moment showing Harry's limits and the nature of the Unforgivable Curses.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film shows Harry casting 'Crucio' at Bellatrix and she does appear to feel pain briefly before escaping. However, Bellatrix's key dialogue explaining that you have to mean it — the moral and thematic core of the scene — is absent. The scene is present but stripped of its lesson.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Bellatrix's 'you have to mean it' line establishes that Harry is not yet capable of the deliberate cruelty required for the Unforgivable Curses — a crucial point about his moral character that distinguishes him from Voldemort. Without it, the scene is just Harry unsuccessfully attacking Bellatrix, losing the thematic dimension entirely.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 8 — Dumbledore vs Voldemort duel: Voldemort possesses Harry
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book scenes 402-408: Voldemort possesses Harry, and Harry — in agony — thinks 'let him kill us… end it, Dumbledore… death is nothing compared to this.' He is only freed when his grief for Sirius floods him, because Voldemort cannot bear to inhabit a body filled with love and grief. Harry's emotional capacity is literally what repels Voldemort. This directly enacts the prophecy's 'power the Dark Lord knows not.'
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film shows Voldemort possessing Harry and Harry cycling through memories of his friends. He then says aloud to Voldemort: 'You're the weak one, and you'll never know love, or friendship. And I feel sorry for you.' Dumbledore says 'It isn't how you are alike, it's how you're not.' Voldemort is repelled. The mechanism is externalised as a speech rather than an involuntary overflow of grief.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is structurally the most damaging change in the film. The book's possession scene enacts the saga's central theme — love as an active, protective magical force — through action and internal experience. Harry doesn't think his way out; he is overwhelmed by grief for Sirius and that involuntary emotional flood is what saves him. The film converts this into a conscious speech of moral superiority ('I feel sorry for you'), which makes Harry's victory a matter of rhetorical confidence rather than the love-as-magic that the entire series has been building toward. Dumbledore's later explanation that 'the power he knows not' is love becomes less coherent because the film hasn't shown it operating that way.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 9 — Dumbledore's explanation to Harry after the battle
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book scenes 416-481: Dumbledore gives Harry an extended, anguished explanation covering: his deliberate distancing from Harry to prevent Voldemort exploiting the connection; his failure to tell Harry about the prophecy across five years; the full content of the prophecy; the meaning of 'the power he knows not'; his own culpability in Sirius's death; the history of Harry's protection through his mother's blood. This is one of the longest and most emotionally significant scenes in the book.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film's Dumbledore tells Harry only: 'I knew it was only a matter of time before Voldemort made the connection between you. I thought by distancing myself from you… he'd be less tempted… I care too much about you.' The prophecy has already been heard by Harry in the Department of Mysteries. The explanation of the power of love, the history of Dumbledore's protective choices, the full moral reckoning with his own failures, and Harry's grief being worked through with Dumbledore are all absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's closing scene between Harry and Dumbledore is the emotional and thematic culmination of the entire novel. It is where the prophecy is contextualised, where Dumbledore's humanity and fallibility are fully revealed, and where Harry begins to understand the true nature of his power. The film's truncated version gives Harry only a brief emotional acknowledgment without the intellectual and moral weight of the book's scene. The saga's central theme — love as the power Voldemort cannot comprehend — is never properly articulated.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 2 — Sirius at King's Cross as Padfoot; photo of the original Order
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book scene 29: Sirius in the book is confined to Grimmauld Place and cannot come to King's Cross. His frustration at being trapped and useless is a running theme. The photo of the original Order is shown by Moody at Grimmauld Place (book scene 70-72), not by Sirius at a train station.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Sirius transforms into a dog and accompanies Harry to King's Cross, where he gives him the Order photo. Moody reproaches him ('Padfoot, are you barking mad? You'll blow the entire operation'). The scene reframes Sirius's recklessness as charming rather than as a symptom of his cabin-fever and poor judgment.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's Sirius is genuinely impaired by his confinement — he makes poor decisions because he is psychologically damaged by years of Azkaban and current imprisonment. The film romanticises his recklessness as loveable swashbuckling, which undermines the book's more tragic portrait of a man who cannot help putting himself and others at risk, and which partly explains how he ends up dead.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 3 — Umbridge's first Defence class: Harry's confrontation
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book scenes 93-95: Harry says 'Voldemort killed him and you know it' in class. The confrontation is about truth-telling in a public institutional setting. Harry is immediately sent to Umbridge's office for detention. The specific words 'It was murder. Voldemort killed him' appear.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film faithfully reproduces Harry's confrontation including 'It was murder. Voldemort killed him! You must know that!' This is faithful. No damage here.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This scene is largely faithful to the book corpus. Minimal damage — flagged only to note the film does preserve Harry's directness and use of Voldemort's name.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 6 — Harry trying to contact Sirius via Umbridge's fireplace; Snape's response
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book scene 329-331: Harry tries to communicate 'Voldemort's got Sirius' to Snape through eye contact. Snape's reaction is described as: he 'looked back at Harry, who stared at him, frantic to communicate without words.' Snape is thrown out by Umbridge before he can act — but the book later reveals he did alert the Order immediately.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film has Snape tell Umbridge: 'I'm afraid you've used up all my stores interrogating students… Unless you wish to poison him… I cannot help you.' He leaves without any indication he has understood Harry's message or will act on it. His cover as a double agent is maintained but the film does not give any hint that Snape acts on Harry's signal.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's version preserves Snape's ambiguity while later confirming he did act to protect Harry. The film's version makes Snape appear simply unhelpful, losing the layered complexity of his character at a moment where his double-agent role is subtly in play.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 3 (Spinner's End / Unbreakable Vow) — Snape's defence of himself collapses to a single boast
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 26-46 establish a lengthy, structured cross-examination in which Bellatrix fires a battery of specific accusations (absence when Voldemort fell, failure to search for him, blocking the Philosopher's Stone, late return at the Dark Mark, protecting Harry, spying within Hogwarts) and Snape answers each in turn with cool, layered counter-arguments. The scene runs for nearly twenty pages and reveals Snape's formidable intelligence, composure under pressure, and the ironical texture of his double life.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film compresses the entire interrogation to a single line: 'Over the years I have played my part well. So well I've deceived one of the greatest wizards of all time.' Bellatrix makes only a brief scathing sound; none of her specific charges are voiced, and none of Snape's elaborate, point-by-point defences are heard.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's interrogation is the richest direct window into Snape's double-agent psychology in the entire novel. Removing it strips him of the forensic intelligence and controlled menace that make the Unbreakable Vow scene so charged. The audience loses the evidence that Snape has rehearsed every angle of his cover story and that Voldemort has already accepted it — context that is essential to understanding Snape's authority in the Death Eater world and to the eventual revelation of his true allegiance.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 3 (Spinner's End) — Narcissa's escalating despair and Snape's reluctance removed
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 47-63 show Narcissa sobbing, clutching Snape's robes, collapsing at his feet, and finally kneeling before him. Snape is visibly uncomfortable with her tears, looks away, and his hand twitches at the third vow — signs of internal conflict. The vow is preceded by Bellatrix's triumphant mockery ('just empty words, the usual slithering out of action') forcing Snape to prove himself.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film's Narcissa is distressed but controlled. There is no collapse, no prolonged physical pleading, no moment of Snape looking away from her tears. Bellatrix's mockery ('It's just empty words. He'll slither back into his hole') is present but brief, and Snape's hand twitch during the third vow is retained — however the surrounding physical and emotional escalation that gives it weight is absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The physical extremity of Narcissa's despair in the book establishes the maternal stakes and the depth of Snape's discomfort — he is not coldly calculating but genuinely affected. Softening this makes the Unbreakable Vow feel more transactional and less morally complex.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 7 (Orphanage — Riddle's room, Pensieve) — Tom Riddle's stolen-objects box reframed
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 253-255: When Dumbledore asks whether the box contains things Riddle ought not to have, Riddle gives 'a long, clear, calculating look' and answers in 'an expressionless voice' — 'Yes, I suppose so, sir.' He shows no remorse. Dumbledore commands him to return each item with an apology and warns that thieving is not tolerated, firmly establishing Riddle's predatory trophy-collecting as a character flaw Dumbledore names and rebukes.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 7: Riddle says 'I like having things that belonged to other people. It makes me feel... close to them.' This reframes compulsive trophy-theft as an orphan's longing for connection — sympathetic rather than sinister. Dumbledore's rebuke ('Thievery is not tolerated') follows but the emotional register of the exchange is softened.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Dumbledore's later analysis (book Scene 281) explicitly connects Riddle's trophy-hoarding to the Horcruxes: objects taken as souvenirs of cruelty, chosen for their magical prestige. The film's 'closeness' line introduces a sympathetic psychological rationale that partially obscures the predatory, power-obsessed logic Dumbledore wants Harry to understand. It slightly dilutes the thematic throughline between young Riddle's behaviour and Voldemort's Horcrux choices.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 8 (Dumbledore's office post-orphanage memory) — Dumbledore's analytical debrief on Riddle's character omitted
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 277-281: After leaving the orphanage memory, Dumbledore delivers a structured analysis pointing out three things Harry must remember — Riddle's contempt for anything that made him ordinary (the name 'Tom'), his self-sufficient secretiveness, and his magpie-like trophy-collecting habit. He frames these explicitly as keys to understanding Voldemort.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 8: Dumbledore's post-memory commentary is replaced with a brief exchange about Slughorn and his possession of a 'particular memory.' The three analytical observations about young Riddle are entirely absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: These observations are not merely interesting biography — Dumbledore is teaching Harry how to think about Voldemort's psychology as a strategic tool. Their absence weakens the film's case for why the private lessons matter and removes the explicit intellectual framework (trophy-collecting → Horcrux object choices) that the book uses to justify the entire memory-gathering project.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 12 (Slughorn memory, first version — fogged) — word 'Horcrux' excised from Riddle's approach
